nort-031.title: The Morasko craters near Poznań
nort-031.text: Near today's Poznań, Poland, a meteorite fall made a field of seven craters about 5,000 years ago. The largest is about 100 m wide. It is one of several small Holocene crater fields in this course, alongside {{ref:nort-019}} and {{ref:megh-016}}.

nort-030.title: Iron falls on Campo del Cielo
nort-030.text: Sometime between about 5,000 and 4,000 years ago, a shower of iron meteorites fell on the plains bordering Argentina's Chaco Province. That strewn field is called Campo del Cielo. It is one of several Holocene meteorite falls in this course, from {{ref:nort-031}} to {{ref:megh-086}}.

megh-001.title: The 4.2-kiloyear drought topples empires
megh-001.text: Nile floods failed, irrigated fields salted up, and kingdoms fell. A severe drought began about 4,200 years ago and, starting around 2200 BC, probably lasted the whole 22nd century BC. It ranks among the Holocene's harshest climate events. Intense aridity is recorded from North Africa and the Middle East to Arabia, India and midcontinental North America. The East Asian summer monsoon weakened sharply. Models link the drought to a major weakening of the Atlantic overturning circulation. The tropical rain belt, the ITCZ, shifted abruptly south. The drought is thought to have helped topple Egypt's Old Kingdom, the Akkadian Empire and China's Liangzhu culture. A stalagmite in India's Mawmluh Cave marks it as the base of the Meghalayan, 4,250 years before 2000. That choice is debated. Critics argue the drought was neither global nor neatly timed, so it makes an awkward boundary.

megh-005.title: The last mammoths die on Wrangel Island
megh-005.text: The last mammoths anywhere lived on an Arctic island. A small population of dwarf woolly mammoths survived on Wrangel Island, in the Siberian Arctic, until about 4,000 years ago. They outlasted mainland mammoths, whose end is told in {{ref:gree-031}}, by some 6,000 years. The latest Wrangel remains are dated to 1795–1675 BCE. Their extinction did not coincide with human arrival; the island had been a human-free refuge.

megh-004.title: The humid period ends across East and equatorial Africa
megh-004.text: In the Sahara, Lake Teli dried out completely about 4,200 years ago. Groundwater-fed Lake Yoa turned hypersaline, far saltier than the sea, by 4,000 years ago. A major pan-tropical environmental change took place around then, and drying in East Africa peaked. Blue Nile discharge fell noticeably. Its sediment load rose as vegetation thinned in the catchment from 4,000–3,600 years ago. The end came later nearer the equator, between 4,000 and 2,500 years ago, and West Africa had a long dry phase 3,500–1,700 years ago. South of the equator, at Lake Malawi, drying began only about 1,000 years ago.

megh-007.title: Mount St. Helens lays down its Yn tephra
megh-007.text: Long before its famous 1980 blast, described in {{ref:megh-102}}, Mount St. Helens had a far larger eruption. About 1860 BCE it laid down its Yn, or Smith Creek, tephra in a VEI 6 eruption of roughly 15 km³. That layer of ash is part of the volcano's long record of violent eruptions.

megh-008.title: The Avellino eruption buries a Bronze Age village
megh-008.text: Near Nola, a hastily abandoned village and thousands of fleeing footprints lie buried under pumice and ash. Around 1800 BC, Vesuvius erupted in the VEI 6 Avellino eruption, one of at least three prehistoric eruptions much larger than that of AD 79. It destroyed several Bronze Age settlements. Pyroclastic surges travelled 15 km northwest of the vent, leaving deposits up to 3 m deep where Naples now stands.

megh-009.title: A weakening monsoon dries the Indus valley
megh-009.text: Most cities of the Indus civilisation were abandoned by about 1700 BCE. Around 4,000 years ago the monsoon-fed Ghaggar-Hakra rivers became seasonal as that civilisation waned. From about 1800 BCE the Indus Valley grew markedly cooler and drier as the monsoon weakened. The Indian summer monsoon stayed weaker from 3,510 to 2,550 BP, apart from a strong interval 3,400–3,200 BP.

megh-010.title: Aniakchak and the frost of 1627 BC
megh-010.text: Frost-damaged tree rings record extreme global cooling in 1627 BC. For years it was blamed on Thera. Then ash in the matching Greenland sulfate spike was matched to Alaska's Mount Aniakchak instead. Aniakchak erupted at VEI 6, ejecting about 50 km³ of material. A 2019 revised Greenland ice-core chronology dates it to 1628 BC.

megh-011.title: The Minoan eruption of Thera
megh-011.text: Minoan Akrotiri was destroyed, and its ash became a marker layer at nearly every eastern Mediterranean site. A catastrophic Plinian eruption, a tall, sustained explosive column, devastated the Aegean island of Thera, or Santorini, around 1600 BC. It left the caldera that forms the island's central bay. Rated VEI 7, it ejected about 28–41 km³ dense-rock equivalent, one of the largest volcanic events in human history. With earthquakes and tsunamis it struck nearby islands and the coast of Crete. Chinese annals of yellow skies and summer frost may record its volcanic winter. Its exact date has been fiercely debated for decades. Radiocarbon favours the 17th–16th century BC, while archaeology points to about 1550–1480 BC.

megh-014.title: The Caribbean's last ground sloths
megh-014.text: Mainland ground sloths had died out about 11,000 years ago, as {{ref:gree-018}} tells. Their island relatives outlived them. Caribbean ground sloths, the group's last survivors, lived on Cuba, Hispaniola and Puerto Rico possibly until 1550 BCE, much as Wrangel Island's mammoths outlasted theirs.

megh-015.title: Did the last litopterns live into the late Holocene?
megh-015.text: Litopterns were an order of South American native hoofed mammals that arose 62.5 million years ago. They are usually thought to have vanished about 12,000 years ago. A 2025 study challenges that. It radiocarbon-dated a Xenorhinotherium specimen to 3,493–4,217 years ago, suggesting the order survived into the late Holocene. That claim rests on a single date, so it remains unconfirmed.

megh-016.title: The Kaali craters form on Saaremaa
megh-016.text: A meteor of 20–80 tonnes broke up in the air over Saaremaa, Estonia, and blasted nine craters. The largest is 110 m across. The blast incinerated vegetation up to 6 km away, and it is one of the few impacts in a populated area. The latest estimates place it shortly after 1530–1450 BC, though published ages vary by up to 6,000 years.

megh-017.title: Thylacine and devil vanish from mainland Australia
megh-017.text: The consensus is that thylacines died out on mainland Australia around 1277–1229 BCE. The latest mainland Tasmanian devil remains share that date. Competition with human hunters and dingoes is the likely cause, with a warming climate also proposed. Both animals survived only in Tasmania, long before European settlement. The thylacine's final end there is told in {{ref:megh-084}}.

megh-019.title: Hekla 3 dusts northern Europe
megh-019.text: Irish tree rings show a decade of stunted growth after one Icelandic eruption. Hekla's H3 eruption, one of Iceland's largest of the Holocene, threw about 7.3 km³ of rock into the atmosphere, a VEI 5 event. Its traces reach Scottish peat bogs, and Hekla's big prehistoric eruptions left date-marker layers across northern Europe. It probably cooled the northern parts of the globe for a few years. Recalibrated with IntCal20, it dates to 1063 ± 140 BCE.

megh-020.title: Pinatubo's Maraunot eruption
megh-020.text: Mount Pinatubo in Luzon erupted at VEI 6 around 1050 BCE, during its Maraunot eruptive period. It ejected about 12.5 km³ of material. The volcano would erupt on that scale again in {{ref:megh-105}}.

megh-023.title: The Homeric solar minimum
megh-023.text: For about two centuries, the Sun went quiet. A deep, persistent grand solar minimum, the Homeric Minimum, lasted from about 800 to 600 BC. It is linked to the Homeric Climate Oscillation, or 2.8 kyr event, when western North America and Europe grew colder; whether they also grew wetter or drier is debated. Germany's Meerfelder Maar records a lasting shift to colder, wetter, windier weather. The Göschenen I glacier advance in the Alps relates to it.

megh-024.title: The central Sahara becomes a lasting desert
megh-024.text: At Libya's Wadi Tanezzuft, rivers kept flowing long after the rains failed. Water stored in dunes and the Tassili mountains fed them until 2,700 years ago, when they finally stopped. By then the central Sahara had become a desert, and it has remained one ever since. Arabia's long drying trend, under way since 7,000–5,000 years ago, continued until 2,700 years ago. Brief humid spells still returned, as in Roman North Africa and around the Dead Sea between 500 BCE and 300 CE. At the Tanezzuft oasis, the drying trend after 1,600 years ago helped end the Garamantian civilisation.

megh-025.title: Raoul Island blasts open the Denham caldera
megh-025.text: At one spot on Raoul Island, 40 m of pumice lies under 80 m of ignimbrite. About 2,200 years ago, a major dacitic explosion on the island, in the Kermadecs, formed the 6.5 by 4 km Denham caldera. Rated VEI 6 and about the size of Krakatoa's 1883 eruption, it left the Fleetwood tephra.

megh-026.title: The Roman Warm Period
megh-026.text: From about 250 BC to AD 400, unusually warm weather prevailed in Europe and the North Atlantic. This was the Roman Warm Period, or Roman Climatic Optimum. Alpine glaciers show AD 100–400 was markedly warmer than the centuries around it, and Iceland had a warm spell from 230 BC to AD 140. Yet a 2019 analysis of a much larger proxy dataset found it was a regional phenomenon, not a globally coherent episode.

megh-027.title: Lake Chad's Bodélé basin dries out
megh-027.text: The largest single source of dust on Earth today is a dried lakebed. Lake Chad shrank to about 5% of its former size. Its deep northern Bodélé basin, cut off from the Chari River, dried out completely about 2,000–1,000 years ago. Its dust is the lasting mark of {{ref:nort-021}}.

megh-028.title: Madagascar loses its giants after people arrive
megh-028.text: At least 17 giant lemur species vanished from Madagascar, nearly all after people colonised the island about 2,000 years ago. Cut-marked bones show humans by 350 BCE, and Bornean Austronesians arrived by 500 CE. The largest animals vanished soon after. Others fell to prolonged hunting as settlers spread about 1,000 years ago, when areas now lemurless held 20 or more lemur species. Malagasy hippos and elephant birds are thought to have died out in 750–1050 AD. The youngest Aepyornis maximus remains date to 1040–1380 CE. Giant lemurs held on into modern times: Megaladapis to 630 ± 50 BP, Palaeopropithecus to 510 ± 80 BP. That makes this one of history's most recent megafaunal extinctions. The land changed too. Aridification began nearly 3,000 years ago, and human-set fires deforested the island.

megh-029.title: Okmok and the cold of 43 BCE
megh-029.text: In 43 BCE, Alaska's Okmok volcano had its second Holocene caldera-forming eruption, rated VEI 6. It sent about 15–16 teragrams of sulfur into the stratosphere, cooling the Northern Hemisphere by 0.7–7.4 °C. With another eruption a year or two earlier, it made 43 BCE and the next two years among the coldest of the last 2,500 years. Cold, famine and failed Nile floods followed. This may have helped end Ptolemaic Egypt amid Rome's crisis, though a direct link is unproven.

megh-030.title: Vesuvius buries Pompeii
megh-030.text: Every Plinian eruption is measured against one: the eruption that destroyed Pompeii. Mount Vesuvius erupted in 79 AD, a VEI 5 event of about 3.2 km³ that killed more than 2,000 people. Collapsing eruption columns sent pyroclastic currents over Herculaneum and Pompeii, and Oplontis and Stabiae were also destroyed. No later Vesuvius eruption was as large.

megh-031.title: Taupō's Hatepe eruption
megh-031.text: Its pyroclastic flow was hot enough to burn forest 160 km from Lake Taupō. The Hatepe, Taupō Volcano's most recent major eruption, is dated to 232 CE ± 10, partly by wiggle-matching the rings of a tree it killed. It ejected roughly 100–120 km³ of material, 30 km³ of it within a few minutes, making it one of the largest eruptions of the last 5,000 years. No one saw it: it struck before people settled New Zealand. Afterwards Lake Taupō refilled and expanded, and temporary lakes formed in the Reporoa basin.

megh-032.title: Ksudach's caldera-forming eruption
megh-032.text: Around 240 CE, Kamchatka's Ksudach volcano had a major caldera-forming eruption, rated VEI 6. It ejected 18–19 km³ and created the 4 by 6.5 km Caldera V. It joins the Kurile Lake caldera of {{ref:gree-049}} among Kamchatka's great Holocene blasts.

megh-033.title: Ilopango's Tierra Blanca Joven eruption
megh-033.text: Lake Ilopango in El Salvador produced the Tierra Blanca Joven eruption around 430 CE, a VEI 6 event of an estimated 37–82 km³. It ranks among the most intense eruptions of the Holocene, alongside Thera, Cerro Blanco and Tambora. Some evidence once made Ilopango the source of the 539/540 eruption of the Late Antique Little Ice Age. A newer study dates it to 431 instead.

megh-035.title: The volcanic winter of 536
megh-035.text: European summers fell up to 2.5 °C below normal. Tree rings show the sharpest cold in mid-July to early August 536 across North America and Eurasia. The extreme weather of 535–536 CE ranks among the notable climate events in Earth history. It is attributed to a large eruption of unknown source around 536, rated VEI 6–7. Its climate impact is compared with Tambora in 1815, Samalas in 1257 and the 1452/1453 mystery eruption. A violent eruption of Krakatoa in 535 was once proposed as the cause. Drilling in the Sunda Strait ruled out an eruption there that year.

megh-034.title: The Late Antique Little Ice Age
megh-034.text: Scandinavia may have lost up to half its population in a century of cold. That cooling of the Northern Hemisphere lasted from AD 536 to about 660, beginning with {{ref:megh-035}}. It coincided with three large eruptions, in 535/536, 539/540 and 547, and one study suggests a global cooling of 2 °C. The second eruption cut European summer temperatures by up to 2.7 °C in 539–540. Sea-ice feedback and a deep solar minimum in the 600s prolonged the cold. It coincided with the Plague of Justinian, which began in 541. It strained the Eastern Roman and Sassanid empires and contributed to the migrations of the Lombards and early Slavs.

megh-037.title: Mount Churchill spreads the White River Ash
megh-037.text: Ash from one Alaskan volcano blankets north-western Canada. Mount Churchill erupted at VEI 6 around 847 CE, ejecting about 50 km³ and laying the eastern lobe of the White River Ash. An earlier VEI 6 eruption, about 145–345 CE, had laid the northern lobe.

megh-039.title: The Millennium eruption of Paektu Mountain
megh-039.text: Ashfall records from Nara suggest the eruption began about 2 November 946. Paektu, or Baekdu, Mountain on the China–North Korea border produced its VEI 6 Millennium eruption that year. It ranks with Thera, Hatepe, Samalas and Tambora among the largest eruptions of the last few thousand years. Its date is unusually exact. Tree rings counted from the 774–775 Miyake carbon spike, together with Greenland ice-core tephra, fix it to late 946.

megh-040.title: The Medieval Warm Period
megh-040.text: The Indo-Pacific Warm Pool stayed warm and saline from 1000 to 1400, with temperatures close to today's, then cooled. A warm spell, the Medieval Warm Period or Medieval Climate Anomaly, lasted from about 950 to 1250, just before the Little Ice Age. Reconstructions show warmth in the eleventh and early fifteenth centuries, though the twentieth century was warmer still. Evidence does not show globally synchronous warmth, so the term has limited use for hemispheric or global trends. The warmth may have sent extra fresh water into the North Atlantic, possibly disrupting ocean circulation ahead of {{ref:megh-046}}.

megh-042.title: Samalas erupts and buries a city on Lombok
megh-042.text: Eruption columns rose 38–43 km over the Indonesian island of Lombok in 1257. Samalas erupted catastrophically, with a VEI of 7, one of the Holocene's largest eruptions. Pyroclastic flows buried much of Lombok, destroyed the city of Pamatan and left the 6–7 km Segara Anak caldera. Ice cores worldwide record a large sulfate spike. The aerosols caused a volcanic winter, cooling by about 0.7 °C in 1258 and 1.2 °C in 1259. Cold, wet weather brought floods, crop failures and famine in Europe and Japan in 1258–1259, though the scale of the anomalies is still debated. The eruption may have helped trigger the Little Ice Age.

megh-045.title: Quilotoa wakes after 14,000 years
megh-045.text: After 14,000 years of dormancy, Quilotoa in Ecuador produced its 1280 Plinian eruption, rated VEI 6. Its collapse left a 3 km caldera. Pyroclastic flows and lahars, volcanic mudflows, reached the Pacific, and ash spread across the northern Andes. With Samalas, it is linked to a cold, dry interval on the South American Altiplano between 1200 and 1450.

megh-046.title: The Little Ice Age
megh-046.text: Mountain glaciers advanced in Europe, Alaska, New Zealand and Patagonia, and Atlantic pack ice grew from about 1250. The Little Ice Age was a period of regional cooling, strongest around the North Atlantic, from about 1300 to about 1850. Despite its name, it was not a true global ice age. Across the Northern Hemisphere it was a modest cooling of under 1 °C relative to late twentieth-century levels. Its regional maxima came at different times. Onset was between 1200 and 1400 in the north and about two centuries later in the south. It ended in the late nineteenth or early twentieth century. Proposed causes include volcanism, low solar activity, ocean circulation changes and human depopulation. Climate models point to volcanism as the main driver, which ties it to eruptions such as {{ref:megh-042}}, {{ref:megh-052}} and {{ref:megh-057}}.

megh-048.title: The last West Indian giant tortoise
megh-048.text: Chelonoidis alburyorum was the last West Indian giant tortoise. It vanished island by island. It lasted on the Abacos to 1170 CE, on Grand Turk to 1200 and on Middle Caicos to about 1400.

megh-051.title: Moa hunted to extinction
megh-051.text: Ovens near the Waitaki River mouth alone held an estimated 29,000–90,000 moa. Moa were nine species of wingless birds up to about 3.6 m tall, New Zealand's largest land animals and dominant herbivores until the Māori arrived. Hunting, and to a lesser degree forest clearance, wiped them out, probably within 100 years of human settlement. Middens, ancient rubbish heaps, hold huge numbers of their bones. By 1445 all moa were gone. Haast's eagle, the giant raptor that had preyed on them, disappeared with them.

megh-052.title: The 1452/1453 mystery eruption
megh-052.text: Central Europe had seven cold summers in the 1450s. The cause was an undocumented eruption in 1452/1453, known mainly from its climate signal; it may have been at Kuwae in Vanuatu. One table rates it VEI 7. It triggered a second pulse of Little Ice Age cooling. With Samalas and Tambora, it was among the strongest cooling events of the last millennium.

megh-056.title: The Grindelwald Fluctuation
megh-056.text: From the 1560s to the 1630s, glaciers at Grindelwald, Switzerland, expanded markedly, part of a worldwide glacial expansion. Temperatures ran 1–2 °C below twentieth-century averages, among the lowest of the Holocene. Eruptions of Colima (1585), Nevado del Ruiz (1595) and Huaynaputina (1600) likely contributed. Yet the cooling began about 15 years before the first of them.

megh-057.title: Huaynaputina, South America's largest witnessed eruption
megh-057.text: On 19 February 1600, Huaynaputina in southern Peru began the largest eruption ever witnessed in South America, rated VEI 6. It killed perhaps 1,000–1,500 people, buried the surrounding land under 2 m of volcanic rock and coated nearby El Misti in ash. Its sulfur cut sunlight by about 1.9 W/m². The summer of 1601 was among the Northern Hemisphere's coldest of the last six centuries. Frosts and harvest failures followed from Sweden to China and Japan, probably including Russia's famine of 1601–1603. With Samalas and the 1452/1453 eruption, it may have helped bring on the Little Ice Age's coldest phase.

megh-058.title: A carbon dioxide dip around 1610
megh-058.text: Conquest and disease killed as many as 90% of Indigenous Americans. Around 50 million hectares of their farmland may have returned to forest. Regrowth of tropical American forests from 1500 to 1650 may have stored 2–5 Pg of carbon. Atmospheric carbon dioxide fell around 1610, a drop that shows in ice at Law Dome, Antarctica. Those mass deaths may explain it, though Huaynaputina's eruption may have contributed. The link is debated: critics argue pre-Columbian farming did not clear forest on a modern scale, so regrowth should have had little effect. A 2015 report suggested 1610 as one possible start of the Anthropocene.

megh-059.title: The last wild aurochs dies in Poland
megh-059.text: The aurochs, the wild ancestor of most modern cattle, once ranged across Eurasia, North Africa and India. Only the European form survived into historical times. Hunting, forest clearance, competition with livestock and cattle diseases left one herd in Poland's Jaktorów forest. The last of them died there in 1627.

megh-060.title: The Maunder Minimum
megh-060.text: From 1645 to 1715 the Sun was unusually quiet. Sunspots were minimal, and deposition of carbon-14 and beryllium-10 rose. This Maunder Minimum fell in the coldest part of the Little Ice Age; one of three especially cold intervals began about 1650. Yet the Sun was not the main cause. Northern Hemisphere cooling began before the minimum, and climate models make volcanism the larger driver.

megh-062.title: The dodo vanishes from Mauritius
megh-062.text: The dodo was a large, flightless relative of pigeons found only on Mauritius. It was last seen in 1662 and may have vanished from the main island by the 1640s. Sailors ate many, but introduced pigs and other species likely did more harm. The dodo became an early poster species for human-caused extinction. Other Mascarene birds followed, including the Réunion rail, last recorded in 1674, the Rodrigues rail in 1726 and the Réunion ibis in 1763.

megh-011.text: An explosive eruption that drives a tall, sustained column of gas and ash high into the sky.

megh-045.text: A volcanic mudflow of ash, rock and water.
